idiom_name: fixed-capacity ring + mutex; policy enum {BLOCK, REJECT, DROP_OLDEST}
implementation_notes: C has no queue in the standard library, so the pattern is the structure itself: a fixed array with head/tail indices plus one policy value, with the admission decision inside the critical section. Blocking is a pthread_mutex_t paired with a pthread_cond_t (or pthread_cond_timedwait for a bounded wait); the reject policy returns a distinct status the caller must handle. Where the queue belongs to the OS, the same decision is already parameterised: mq_send blocks while the queue is full, mq_timedsend bounds the wait (ETIMEDOUT) and O_NONBLOCK converts fullness into EAGAIN, so the hand-written structure is justified mainly when you need a drop/coalesce policy, watermarks or per-item attribution.
pitfalls: Doing work under the mutex (or holding it while signalling): the drain side stalls and the ring looks full even when the consumer is keeping up.
Condition-variable misuse - a different mutex, no predicate loop, or signal where broadcast is needed - turns a bounded wait into a lost wakeup and a hung producer.
Storing pointers bounds the count but not the memory: the retained payload is unbounded until the consumer frees it, so the capacity must cover the bytes, not just the items.
